title: Cancelling a coaching or break request by id redirects to the request's program even when it is not the caller's
description: requests_coaching_cancel reads the change request for any request_id, then changes.cancel refuses unless the caller is the requester, but the route still redirects to /requests/coaching?program=<row program>. A non-associate with approve_tm or rta_change can enumerate integer ids and learn each request's program name from the Location header, against the Phase AR rule that refusals must not reveal program names. Verified by an independent reviewer: break_changes.py:116 loads the row for any id (store.py:1217-1220 bare select) with no program/ownership check; changes.cancel (change_requests.py:637-638) refuses non-requesters but the exception is only flashed and line 122 still 303-redirects to requests_coaching?program=row['program']. Sibling request_change_decide (188-189) calls can_open(row['program']); the cancel route omits it. Phase AR wall (app.py:399) bypassed for the program name. Real impact: A user limited to one program can learn which program any coaching/break request id belongs to, and which ids exist, from the 303 Location header. Low-sensitivity cross-program metadata leak; nothing modified. Preconditions: Authenticated non-associate with approve_tm or rta_change; Valid session and CSRF token; Sequential integer request ids; Target request in a program the caller cannot open. Corrections: Trace/evidence lines accurate (decorator 110-112, function 112). Location header is also an id existence oracle: missing id redirects without program param (break_changes.py:122, row None); existing id redirects with program=<name>.
claimed_root_cause: The redirect uses the row's program before authorising the row (no can_open or ownership check ahead of the read).

title: RTA day POST routes authorize one program but act on another (query string versus form field)
description: The global program wall checks request.values.get('program'). On a POST Werkzeug builds request.values from the query string first, then the form. Almost every /day/* POST handler then reads request.form.get('program') and passes it to DayBook without re-checking can_open. A user with rta_change and one program (Planner and Supervisor by default) could POST /day/break?program=<own> with form program=<other> and edit another program's RTA day, read previews, or trigger group posts to its channel. With ?program= empty the wall is skipped. Verified by an independent reviewer: app.py:396-397 derives the key from request.values.get('program') and 403s only if can_open fails; a non-empty ?program=<own> passes, while _day_form (day.py:678) and _posted_day (day.py:682) read request.form['program'] and day_break (791-802) passes it to DayBook.move_break (attendance.py:1268) with no can_open. An empty ?program= skips the wall (app.py:397). Real impact: A planner or supervisor restricted to some programs can read previews and change RTA day data (breaks, statuses, channel moves, bulk changes, possibly group posts) of programs they were not granted, breaking the per-program isolation (app.py:399-400). Needs a normal account plus a crafted POST. Preconditions: Authenticated non-admin, non-all_programs user (planner or supervisor) with the role permission for the day endpoint; Valid CSRF token from their own session (check_csrf runs first, app.py:368); Target program key exists with a date in range and an associate name in it; Werkzeug args-then-form order on POST (library fact), or empty ?program= skipping the wall. Corrections: day_break sink is attendance.py:1268 (move_break); set_status at 1189; both take a raw program string with no user/can_open check. Role gate is PERMISSION_ENDPOINTS at app.py:377 (permissions.py:37 lists day_break): role only, not program. The wall (app.py:394-401) skips OPEN_TO_ALL; no /day/* write endpoint is in that set, so the only program check is on request.values. _route_to_lob (app.py:420-432) rewrites form program only for merge=1 merged units: not a control. Only day_operating_start (day.py:622), day_absences (day.py:770), day_shrinkage_map (analytics.py:169) re-check can_open. Access.can_open returns True for admins/all_programs, so the gap matters only for restricted users. No code overrides request_class/values, so Werkzeug's default (args then form) applies; not opened here.
claimed_root_cause: Policy and sink disagree on where 'program' comes from: the wall reads request.values (args first), handlers read request.form, and DayBook has no user awareness.

title: Role back-limit on RTA edits can be bypassed with a per-move date in Replan/Rescue apply
description: Owner rule (Phase AY, comment above DAY_WRITES in routes/day.py): a planner or team manager may change today and 1 day back, a supervisor 7 days back, only an admin without limit. The gate (_still_editable, called from the global before_request) inspects only the form fields 'date' and 'first'. POST /day/replan/apply and /day/rescue/apply accept repeated 'move' items 'name|idx|minute|YYYY-MM-DD' (_move_item); the embedded date goes straight to DayBook.move_break and is never re-checked against the caller's back limit. A planner could post date=today with a move dated months back and rewrite actual_breaks (and the day log and group-post queue) of a closed day on a program they can open. A smaller variant: /day/bulk/apply accepts a form 'start' of up to +/-9999 minutes (about 7 days) shifting which shift dates change. Same principal and program, but it crosses the role hierarchy the owner defined. Verified by an independent reviewer: The only back-limit gate is app.py:384-386, checking request.form 'date' and 'first' via _still_editable (day.py:1212-1221). day_replan_apply (966) and day_rescue_apply (988) take per-item dates from _move_item (938-947); apply_replan (attendance.py:2138) and apply_rescue (2392) pass them to move_break (1268), which only needs a schedule version and the person's shift on that date, plus check_break, then writes set_actual_break and _log. No role or date-age check, so a Planner (back limit 1) can post date=today with an older move date and edit a closed day. Real impact: A planner or team manager (1-day limit) or supervisor (7-day limit) can rewrite actual_breaks, day_log entries and group-post notifications for dates older than their role allows, in a program they can already open. It defeats the owner's role-hierarchy rule, and changes outside on-1..on+1 may fall outside Undo. Preconditions: Authenticated non-admin with the permission mapped to day_replan_apply or day_rescue_apply (rta_change, default on for Planner); Program access and a valid CSRF token; A schedule version covering the old date, the named associate on a shift that date and a plan break at that idx; Move date within _date bounds; check_break rules satisfied. Corrections: day_replan_apply is routes/day.py:958-978 (its _move_item call at 966); _move_item 938; DAY_WRITES 1182; _back_limit 1206; _still_editable 1212; app.py gate 384-386. day_rescue_apply (day.py:980-996) also feeds per-move dates to apply_rescue (attendance.py:2358); its `now` guard compares minutes relative to `on` only, so it does not stop an older move date. The /day/bulk/apply 'start' variant (_form_start, day.py:933) was not traced; secondary at most.
claimed_root_cause: The back-date authorisation is enforced only on two request fields (date, first) in the central hook, while the data layer (apply_replan, apply_rescue, apply_bulk -> move_break) accepts any in-range date supplied per item and does not know the caller's role limit; the journal records only on-1..on+1, so such changes are not undoable.

title: Lockout failure counter is a lost-update race, so concurrent guesses exceed 5 per lock
description: Waitress serves with 8 threads and hashlib.scrypt releases the GIL, so a burst of concurrent wrong guesses against one account read the same counter and each writes the same increment. The counter advances about once per batch, so more than 5 guesses (up to ~8 per step) can be tried per 15-minute lock. Requests past the locked check still verify a password after the lock is set. The same function backs change_password's current-password check. The per-IP throttle is checked only before authenticate and admits one in-flight burst. Bounded multiple (low) on online guessing against one account. Verified by an independent reviewer: authenticate (store.py:948-973) is read-verify-write on a private connection with no begin immediate (952-967) and no in-process lock; the only sign-in locks are in throttle.py. Waitress runs 8 threads and scrypt sits between read (953) and absolute write (965), so concurrent wrong guesses can share a stale counter and a stale write can zero locked_until. Open fact: whether hashlib.scrypt releases the GIL and threads overlap on the deployed build. Real impact: The 5-guess per 15-minute lockout can be exceeded (roughly up to 8 guesses per counter step) and a lock can be overwritten back to unlocked by a stale write: a modest multiple of online guessing against one account. It does not bypass authentication; password policy and scrypt cost still bound the gain. Preconditions: Attacker can POST /login with no account; knowing a username is enough; Burst of up to 8 concurrent requests against one username; Per-IP throttle not yet held; addresses can be rotated; Real thread overlap during scrypt. Corrections: Lines hold (sign_in.py:27,31,33-34; store.py:953,961-962,963,965-966; _db 604-637; transaction() begin immediate 640-651; serve.py:58; check_password 998-999; sign_in.py:79). Impact understated: the stale UPDATE (store.py:965-966) also writes locked_until. A thread that read failed=N before another set the lock writes (failed=N+1, locked_until=0), so it can erase an existing lock, not only slow the counter. Per-IP throttle (throttle.py:13, 40 per 15 min; held 26-29) is checked before and recorded after authenticate (sign_in.py:27,34), so a burst of 8 in flight overshoots slightly; it does nothing against many addresses. The authenticate read is a plain select on an autocommit-style connection, so no read lock spans scrypt: confirms the race window.
claimed_root_cause: authenticate reads users.failed, runs scrypt, then writes failed+1 as an absolute value on separate sqlite connections with no write transaction or atomic increment.

Reads user row (failed, locked_until) in its own connection; no begin immediate.

title: Username enumeration by timing: padded passwords take two scrypt checks only for real, unlocked accounts
description: For unknown or locked usernames authenticate does one dummy scrypt check. For a real unlocked account it checks the typed password and, when the cleaned form differs (leading/trailing space, tab, NBSP, zero-width), checks again. A padded guess costs ~2x scrypt for a real unlocked account and 1x otherwise, so an unauthenticated caller can tell which usernames exist (and whether one is locked) though messages are identical. Each probe counts on the IP throttle (40 per 15 min). Low impact: usernames of staff accounts. Verified by an independent reviewer: store.py:954-959 does one scrypt check (against _DUMMY_HASH, store.py:465, same method) for unknown or locked usernames; 961-962 does a second check when clean_password(typed) != typed (store.py:447-450 strips space, tab, newline, NBSP, zero-width at both ends), so a padded wrong password costs two scrypt computations only for real unlocked accounts. Nothing equalises this; the IP throttle (sign_in.py:27, 33-34) caps probes but does not mask timing. Whether ~2x is measurable over the network is an execution/deployment fact. Real impact: An unauthenticated caller can distinguish existing unlocked usernames from unknown or locked ones, defeating the identical-message design (Phase BF). Staff usernames only; no credential access. Preconditions: Unauthenticated access to POST /login; Padding such as a space in the password; Enough samples per username to separate one from two scrypt costs within ~40 failures per 15 min per address (more with distributed sources); Guessed candidate username. Corrections: Line 954 is the row-is-None test; the dummy check is at 955 (locked branch: test 957, dummy 958); sink spans 960-962. login also runs get_user_by_name (:23) and add_event (:36): extra small DB timing differences, not the claimed cause. Scope wider: for a real account a wrong padded password also writes the failed counter (store.py:965), so five padded guesses lock a real account, making lock state observable with identical text.
claimed_root_cause: Dummy-hash equalisation covers one hash, but the real path performs a second hash when clean_password(typed) != typed, so work differs by input.

trace.description: Username and attacker-padded password go to authenticate; response identical, latency differs.
Unknown username: one check against dummy hash, return.
Locked account: one dummy hash check, return.
Existing unlocked account: check on typed string then on cleaned string when it differs: two scrypt computations.

evidence.description: Comment states the intent: one check as for a real name with a wrong password.
clean_password strips spaces, tabs, line breaks, NBSP and zero-width characters at both ends, so a padded password always triggers the second check.

title: A supervisor can reset the password of, and so take over, a user who also holds programs the supervisor does not have
description: Access.can_manage lets a manager with People (Supervisor by default) act on any non-admin, non-supervisor, non-all_programs user who shares at least one program. A planner, team manager or associate holding A and B is manageable by a supervisor who holds only A. Reset creates a temporary password flashed to the supervisor, who can sign in as that user and reach program B and the target's permissions. Disable, delete, switch-off and program changes are allowed by the same gate. Verified by an independent reviewer: access.py:71 returns bool(self.program_ids() & target program ids), a non-empty-intersection test; only admin, supervisor and all_programs targets are excluded (65, 69-70). admin_user_action (people_file.py:236-248) gates only on manager_required and can_manage, then resets at 274-279 with no further check; bulk switch at 224 uses the same gate; sign-in has no restriction. Open question: whether shared-program management is intended policy (can_manage docstring 'supervisors the planners who share a program', access.py:60; test_programs.py:130-144 covers only disjoint and same-program). Real impact: A supervisor can set a temporary password on a user who also holds programs outside the supervisor's scope and sign in as them (must_change lets the supervisor choose a permanent password), reaching the other programs' data and the target's permissions, defeating per-program isolation. The same gate allows disable, delete, unlock and team reassignment of such users. Preconditions: Authenticated supervisor, or a role granted 'people' (permissions.py:30, supervisor by default); Non-admin, non-supervisor, non-all_programs target sharing at least one program and also holding a program the attacker lacks; Target active, or enabled by the attacker via 'enable'. Corrections: people_file.py:278 is the flash of the temporary password; set_password is at 276; 274 is the 'reset' branch header. admin.py:70 is the _chosen_programs docstring: the code anticipates partial overlap only for program edits (keep=), not reset/disable/delete. The 'programs' action is already safe: _chosen_programs (admin.py:77-80) limits grants to the manager's programs and keeps the target's others. Exposure is reset, disable, delete, unlock, bulk switch and team.
claimed_root_cause: The management rule tests intersection of program sets (any shared program), not containment of the target's programs in the manager's.

True if people on, target not admin/supervisor, and manager everything() or program_ids & target program ids non-empty; all_programs targets excluded, supersets not.

title: A user removed from a program keeps read, edit, in-use and delete control over the runs and schedule versions they uploaded into it
description: Run-scoped routes authorise by _can_see_run, which returns True for the uploader without checking current program access, and the global program wall inspects only a 'program' request value. After an admin removes a program from a user, the user can still open and download the run's workbooks, run_start new runs under that program, change the run's week or detach its program, delete it, edit its schedule versions, and set one of its versions in use. set_in_use clears in_use on every version of that program and week, so the former member can change which schedule the program's RTA and day pages use. This contradicts the Phase AR rule that nothing of another program is visible and goes beyond the read-only note from wave 1. Verified by an independent reviewer: app.py:445-446 returns True for the uploader before any can_open check. _run_or_404 (runs.py:54) and _version_or_404 (schedule_versions.py:37) rely on it; the wall (app.py:394-401) is skipped for path-id routes (no 'program' value). _may_set_in_use and _may_delete (schedule_versions.py:41-48) test only admin or uploader. set_user_programs (store.py:679) does not reassign or revoke the user's runs, and test_ar_walls.py covers only users who still hold the program. Real impact: A user removed from a program (reassignment or offboarding) keeps read, download, delete and edit access to the runs and schedule versions they uploaded for it, and can set their version in use, flipping the program's live schedule for the week and so the RTA and day pages of a program they no longer belong to. Exposure limited to the uploader's own runs; the integrity effect on other members' pages is the main concern. Preconditions: User uploaded a run into a program, then an admin or supervisor removed that program from the account; not admin, no all_programs; Role still allows runs, schedules_view, schedules_change (default planner does); User keeps the run or schedule id (own run list, bookmarks; _visible app.py:453 keeps these rows in lists). Corrections: All cited lines match (app.py:445-448, 450-453, 394-401; schedule_versions.py:32-48; week_channels.py:256-264; schedules.py:746-758; runs.py:347). Not read by the verifier: runs.py:351 start_from and schedule_delete.py:22 (plausible but unchecked). Impact narrower: schedule_in_use needs the row's own run user_id == caller, so the former member only affects versions of runs they uploaded. set_in_use scopes by row program and week_start (schedules.py:749-755), so it clears in_use on versions uploaded by OTHER users in the same program and week: the cross-user effect that matters. run_tag (runs.py:337-338, 347) lets the uploader change week_start or clear the program without can_open; moving it to a program they cannot open is blocked.
claimed_root_cause: _can_see_run (and _visible) grant access on run.user_id == current user before and instead of checking the user's current program access; path-id routes never re-check can_open on the run's stored program; permission-matrix checks are role-wide, not program-wide; write-side checks (_may_set_in_use, _may_delete) test only uploader-or-admin; run_tag/start_from skip can_open when the program is unchanged or copied.

title: A swap offer can be answered by an associate of another program who has the same roster name
description: SwapBook.answer authorises the answering user by is_associate and roster_name == row['other'] only; the offer side resolves the colleague with account(program, name). _roster_problem forbids duplicate roster names only across overlapping programs, so identically named associates in different programs can exist, and one could POST /me/swap/<id>/answer on another program's swap (sequential integer ids) and push it to waiting_tm instead of the real colleague. Verified by an independent reviewer: SwapBook.answer (swaps.py:255-258) authorises only on is_associate and roster_name == row['other']; it never checks the swap's program or the program-bound account that offer() resolved (:216-222, :233). _roster_problem (admin.py:64-67) rejects duplicate roster names only when accounts share a program, so same-named associates in disjoint programs are allowed. Trace holds; only whether such duplicates exist in deployed data is open. Real impact: An associate of a different program can accept or decline another program's pending swap in the real colleague's place, forging consent or blocking the swap; the real colleague can then no longer answer. Both teams' manager approval still gates the schedule change: integrity/consent bypass, not a direct roster change. Preconditions: Authenticated active associate whose roster_name equals the target colleague's; Disjoint programs (admin.py:65-66 blocks overlapping); A swap in waiting_other whose 'other' matches that name; ids sequential; Production roster-name collisions across programs. Corrections: Sink is store.move_swap at swaps.py:259-260 (258 is the raise); entry my_week.py:206-212 is login_required only. Impact narrower than described: _sides() (swaps.py:275) resolves the real colleague via account(row['program'], row['other']), so the real colleague's team manager still must approve; the wrong person only decides the colleague's consent step.
claimed_root_cause: Ownership check keyed on a non-unique display roster name instead of the program-bound account found at offer time.

Raises only if not is_associate or roster_name != row['other'].

title: Volumes and people-sheet xlsx reader materialises every row before the row cap and may pad to a forged sheet dimension
description: _rows in bulk_users.py reads the first sheet read-only and iterates iter_rows with no max_row/max_col, building the whole list before read_table's 400,000-row or read_people's 500-row cap applies. In read-only mode openpyxl takes bounds from the uploader-controlled dimension tag and pads missing rows, so a tiny file claiming A1:XFD1048576 may yield a huge number of wide empty tuples. Reached by volumes check and people bulk upload. Availability only, signed-in user with volumes or user-management access. Verified by an independent reviewer: bulk_users.py:98-99 builds the full list with unbounded ws.iter_rows(values_only=True) on a read-only worksheet; both callers (volumes_io.py:63 via volumes.py:458, and people_file.py:110) check row count only afterwards. Sibling volumes_draft.py:114 bounds the read, showing the omission. Whether openpyxl pads to a forged dimension is a library fact source cannot show. Real impact: A low-privilege signed-in user can make one request build a huge in-memory row list: high memory/CPU or an OOM-killed worker (availability only). Preconditions: Authenticated user reaching POST /volumes/actuals/check for a program they may open, or a manager for /admin/users/bulk; Non-draft .xlsx; Web worker with limited memory or request timeout. Corrections: Lines accurate (volumes.py:439-458, volumes_io.py:59-65, bulk_users.py:90-99, people_file.py:110). Forged-dimension padding is not needed: zip_problem (zipcheck.py:11-35) allows up to 250 MB expanded, 150 MB/member, ratio test only above 20 MB; a genuinely dense sheet within limits already becomes a multi-million-row list before the caps (volumes_io.py:64, bulk_users.py:123). The 500-row people cap applies to filtered output after every row is built (107-123). MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH 25 MB bounds only the request. In volumes_actuals_check, is_draft (volumes_draft.py:190-196) runs first and opens read-only without iterating; only non-draft uploads reach read_table. The draft path uses bounded _sheets (volumes_draft.py:114), unaffected.
claimed_root_cause: Shared reader _rows has no row or column bound on iter_rows (unlike volumes_draft._sheets); row-count limits are enforced only after the whole sheet is in memory.

trace.description: POST /volumes/actuals/check; upload read in full (452) and passed to read_table (458).
Calls _rows, checks len(rows) > MAX_ROWS only after all rows exist.
[[cell for cell in row] for row in ws.iter_rows(values_only=True)] on read-only worksheet, unbounded; people upload reaches it via webapp/routes/people_file.py:110.

Sibling reader passes max_col=17 and max_row=MAX_SHEET_ROWS+50; _rows does not.
zip_problem limits expanded size; a forged dimension tag adds no bytes.

Role gating of the volumes check (who can reach it)
Web process memory cap and timeout

title: Run upload workbooks that pass zipcheck can expand to hundreds of MB and are fully loaded by openpyxl in the web process
description: A signed-in user who may upload a schedule workbook can send a ~25 MB .xlsx whose sheet XML expands to up to 150 MB per member and 250 MB total. It passes zip_problem and upload_guard.look (read-only, stops at 400k cells). The web process then opens it with the full non-read-only openpyxl loader (check_ready, read_inputs via the channel check). Memory can be many times the expanded XML. Availability only, authenticated uploader; no MemoryMax in the unit. Verified by an independent reviewer: zipcheck.py:12-13,32-33 caps expanded size at 150 MB per member / 250 MB total and upload_guard.py:106,131 reads read-only with a 400k-cell stop, so nothing bounds what runs.py:152 (read_inputs, day.py:175) and runs.py:307 (check_ready, ready.py:23) materialise. Route is login_required only (runs.py:105), no per-user upload rate limit seen, and no MemoryMax in deploy/scheduler-web.service (Restart=on-failure only). ORACLE_SETUP_GUIDE.md:20 states a 24 GB host. Real peak memory depends on openpyxl version and host. Real impact: An authenticated uploader can drive the shared web process to very high memory or an OOM kill, taking the site down for all users until systemd restarts it (5 s). Availability only. Preconditions: Valid login and access to POST /runs; Crafted .xlsx with required tabs whose sheet XML expands to ~150 MB per member / 250 MB total under the 25 MB body limit; No mandatory memory cap on the service; host OOM behaviour decides impact; Several concurrent uploads multiply memory. Corrections: All cited lines check out (runs.py:106/142/147/152, zipcheck.py:12-13,32-33, upload_guard.py:106 and 131, day.py:175, ready.py:23, volumes_draft.py:114, app.py:281). Ready-schedule path is stronger: RunQueue.submit_ready (runs.py:307) calls check_ready synchronously inside the POST /runs request, so the full non-read-only load happens in the Waitress web process after the only post-zipcheck gate (upload_guard.look). look() stops at 400k cells, but sparse or styled-empty 150 MB XML still passes; later non-read-only loaders materialise every cell. Ratio check (100x) applies only above 20 MB expanded; under 25 MB compressed an expansion of ~10x (250 MB) is allowed.
claimed_root_cause: zipcheck caps (250 MB total, 150 MB per member, ratio check only above 20 MB) are sized to avoid a zip bomb, not for peak memory of a non-read-only openpyxl load; no cell-count or dimension cap before that load.

trace.description: POST /runs saves upload to _incoming; body limit 25 MB (app.py:281).
Accepts up to 2000 members, 150 MB/member, 250 MB total, ratio 100 only above 20 MB.
Read-only, stops after 400k cells; does not limit what later loaders materialise.
_channel_upload_check calls has_channel_needs then read_inputs on a copy.
load_workbook(path, data_only=True) without read_only; ready path does same at webapp/ready.py:23.

check_ready uses load_workbook(path) in the web process.
Contrast: draft reader bounds max_row/max_col and uses read_only.

blockers: Actual MemoryMax/OOM policy and RAM of the live host (guide says 24 GB)
Any upstream rate limit or per-user concurrency gate (Caddy, login limits)
Largest legitimate workbook to set caps safely
Peak RSS of non-read-only openpyxl load for ~150 MB sheet XML on the installed version

title: Schedule version download writes a planner's free-text change reason into the Version Notes sheet as a live formula
description: Anyone with schedules_change can type a reason when changing, swapping, planning breaks or planning channels on a schedule version. The reason is stored after whitespace collapse and truncation (300 chars). When another person downloads an edited version, versions.with_notes writes the reason, validator problem text and version label into the first 'Version Notes' tab with ws.cell(r, c, v). Neither with_notes nor the routes neutralise a leading '=', '+', '-' or '@', unlike exports.py, daily_views.py and bulk_users.py. Under openpyxl a string starting with '=' is stored as a formula, so a reason such as =HYPERLINK(...) becomes a formula in the workbook an admin or supervisor opens in Excel. The Schedules page shows the same text escaped as HTML, so only the Excel download is affected. Effect depends on openpyxl typing and Excel behaviour. Verified by an independent reviewer: versions.py:739 and :730 write reason and problem text with ws.cell(r, c, v) and no neutraliser; week_channels.py:218/246/172 only collapse whitespace and truncate. Sibling exports neutralise (exports.py:503-508, bulk_users.py:40, daily_views.py:60), so this path is the outlier. test_bg_security.py:224 checks formula cells in downloads but may not cover an edited-version download. openpyxl typing a leading '=' string as a formula is library behaviour not visible in this repo. Real impact: A planner can plant a formula such as =HYPERLINK(...) in the Version Notes tab of a workbook that supervisors or admins download and open: a click-to-phish or external-link lure delivered from the trusted site. Needs user interaction in Excel and is limited by Protected View. Preconditions: Attacker holds schedules_change (permissions.py:20, two of three roles) and can reach a schedule version in their program; A different user with schedules_view downloads an edited version via /schedules/<id>/download, with or without tz; The victim opens the workbook in Excel without blocking the formula (Protected View and external-link prompts apply); openpyxl must type the string as 'f'. Corrections: Save-path reasons are cut to 200 chars (week_channels.py:172), not 300; schedule_change (:218) and swap (:246) use 300. Sink is ws.cell(r, c, v) at versions.py:739 (reason is the 7th value at :738); problem text :730; version label :715 inside the lines loop :722-724. Download call sites week_channels.py:283 and :296. ScheduleBook.change is at schedules.py:420 (reason to store.add_change at :435), not :481. The reason is also reused by auto-generated paths (swap_week_days, save_channels) but all take the same planner-typed reason.
claimed_root_cause: with_notes passes user-controlled free text (schedule_changes.reason, validator problem text carrying associate names, version label) straight to openpyxl Worksheet.cell without the formula neutraliser the other export paths apply, so text beginning with '=' is saved as a formula cell in a workbook delivered to a different, possibly higher-privileged user.

title: One forecast request with a large typed total can pin a server thread on quadratic Erlang arithmetic
description: Any signed-in non-associate who can open a program with saved history and a service-level measure can GET /volumes?tab=forecast&total=5000000 (the cap _whole accepts) or the downloads taking the same parameters. VolumeBook.forecast spreads the total over intervals and calls erlang.agents_needed per non-empty Phone or Chat interval. That function increments n one agent at a time and, for each n, service_level runs the Erlang recursion over all n agents: about quadratic in the interval's traffic (roughly 0.15 x T^2 steps for T Erlangs). At the cap, peak intervals can reach tens of thousands of Erlangs, hundreds of millions of Python steps per interval and many intervals per page. A few such requests could hold the 8 Waitress threads and the GIL, slowing the whole site. The default role matrix gives volumes_view to supervisors, planners and team managers. Verified by an independent reviewer: routes/volumes.py:265-270 passes the typed total to vb.forecast; volumes.py:716 and 74 accept any whole number up to 5,000,000; _needs (526-529) calls erlang.agents_needed for every non-zero Phone interval; erlang.py:80-84 steps n one agent at a time and each step runs service_level, which runs the erlang_c loop at erlang.py:43: quadratic in the interval's traffic with no iteration, time or traffic cap. Only bound is MAX_TOTAL; serve.py:58 shows 8 threads in one process and no visible request timeout. The docstring (erlang.py:6-7) claims large centres take no noticeable time, untested at this scale. Real impact: An authenticated low-privilege user can make one GET with a large total burn CPU for minutes or longer; a few concurrent requests can exhaust the 8 worker threads and the GIL, making the site unresponsive for everyone. No data disclosure or integrity impact. Preconditions: Authenticated user with volumes_view and access to a program (default for supervisors, planners, team managers); Program has Phone or Chat history and a service-level measure; Typed total large enough for tens of thousands of Erlangs per interval (5,000,000 per week, ~336 intervals at 15 min, AHT 300 s: mean ~33,000 Erlangs); Several concurrent requests to occupy all 8 threads; one request already holds the GIL for long; No response cache or request timeout in front (Caddy config not read). Corrections: MAX_TOTAL is volumes.py:35; drivers.py:38 has a second MAX_TOTAL = 5_000_000 used by _whole_total (drivers.py:313-318) for other typed totals. _needs call sites volumes.py:528 (Phone) and 531 (Chat); a second agents_needed call at volumes.py:1068/1071 was not in the trace and may be a further sink on download paths. Download routes pass total=request.args.get('total') at routes/volumes.py:686 and 729. Per-interval cost is ~0.14*T^2 steps (n runs from floor(T)+1 to ~T/occupancy); the hunter's 0.15 is approximate. erlang_c loop of int(agents) steps is accurate (erlang.py:43, 55, 82).
claimed_root_cause: erlang.agents_needed searches upward one agent at a time and recomputes service_level, whose Erlang C helper is O(agents), so cost is O(T^2); the only input bound is MAX_TOTAL = 5,000,000 per week (or per typed day), with no per-request time, iteration or traffic cap, contrary to the module's claim that large centres take no noticeable time.

trace.description: GET /volumes?tab=forecast&total=N passes the typed total to vb.forecast; volumes_page needs only volumes_view and program access (permissions.py:51).
_whole accepts any whole number up to 5,000,000 (also per typed day); F.forecast_week spreads it over the history's interval profile.
For every non-empty Phone interval calls erlang.agents_needed (Chat the same at line 531), then service_level again.
while loop increments n by one and recomputes service_level each time; service_level calls erlang_c whose loop at line 43 runs int(agents) steps: O(T^2) with no cap or deadline.

evidence.description: erlang_c loops range(1, int(agents) + 1) on every call.
agents_needed re-evaluates service_level inside the while condition for each candidate n, from floor(traffic)+1 to near traffic / occupancy cap.
MAX_TOTAL = 5_000_000 is the only bound on a typed week total; RANGES allows occupancy down to 50 percent and AHT up to 7200 s, raising cost further.
Waitress runs with threads=8 in one process; no per-request timeout visible in source.
